claim: p27Kip1 (p27) is a cyclin-CDK inhibitor and negative regulator of cell proliferation.
source: p27Kip1 (p27) is a cyclin-CDK inhibitor and negative regulator of cell proliferation.
evidence: This is a well-established characterization of p27 supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: p27 controls cellular processes including migration.
source: p27 also controls other cellular processes including migration
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Cytoplasmic p27 can act as an oncogene.
source: cytoplasmic p27 can act as an oncogene
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies in the introduction.

claim: Cytoplasmic p27 promotes invasion and metastasis, in part by promoting epithelial to mesenchymal transition.
source: Furthermore, cytoplasmic p27 promotes invasion and metastasis, in part by promoting epithelial to mesenchymal transition.
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: p27 promotes cell invasion by binding to and regulating the activity of Cortactin.
source: we find that p27 promotes cell invasion by binding to and regulating the activity of Cortactin, a critical regulator of invadopodia formation
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the results section.

claim: p27 localizes to invadopodia.
source: p27 localizes to invadopodia
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2.

claim: p27 limits invadopodia number and activity.
source: p27 localizes to invadopodia and limits their number and activity
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3 showing increased invadopodia in p27-null cells.

claim: p27 promotes the interaction of Cortactin with PAK1.
source: p27 promotes the interaction of Cortactin with PAK1
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5B-C.

claim: PAK1 promotes invadopodia turnover by phosphorylating Cortactin.
source: In turn, PAK1 promotes invadopodia turnover by phosphorylating Cortactin
evidence: Supported by data with Cortactin mutants and PAK inhibitors in Figures 6-8.

claim: Expression of Cortactin mutants for PAK-targeted sites abolishes p27's effect on invadopodia dynamics.
source: expression of Cortactin mutants for PAK-targeted sites abolishes p27's effect on invadopodia dynamics
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 8 showing effects of Cortactin S113A and triple mutants.

claim: In absence of p27, cells exhibit increased invadopodia stability due to impaired PAK1-Cortactin interaction.
source: Thus, in absence of p27, cells exhibit increased invadopodia stability due to impaired PAK1-Cortactin interaction
evidence: Supported by invadopodia lifetime measurements in Figure 5A and PAK1-Cortactin co-IP in Figure 5C.

claim: p27-null cells have reduced invasive capacity compared to wild-type cells despite increased invadopodia stability.
source: but their invasive capacity is reduced compared to wild-type cells
evidence: Supported by invasion assay data in Figure 4.

claim: p27 directly promotes cell invasion by facilitating invadopodia turnover via the Rac1/PAK1/Cortactin pathway.
source: Overall, we find that p27 directly promotes cell invasion by facilitating invadopodia turnover via the Rac1/PAK1/Cortactin pathway.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study supported by multiple experiments throughout the results section.

claim: p27-mediated cyclin-CDK inhibition involves the N-terminal extremity (aa 28–89) of the protein.
source: p27-mediated cyclin-CDK inhibition involves the N-terminal extremity (aa 28–89) of the protein that allows interaction with both cyclin and CDK subunits (Ou et al., 2012; Besson et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: p27 knockout mice exhibit a hyperproliferative phenotype in multiple tissues.
source: The critical role of p27 as a negative regulator of cell proliferation is underscored by the phenotype of p27 knockout mice, which exhibit a hyperproliferative phenotype in multiple tissues and are more susceptible to tumor development than wild-type animals (Fero et al., 1996; Kiyokawa et al., 1996; Nakayama et al., 1996; Besson et al., 2006; Fero et al., 1998)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to mouse model studies.

claim: p27 knockout mice are more susceptible to tumor development than wild-type animals.
source: The critical role of p27 as a negative regulator of cell proliferation is underscored by the phenotype of p27 knockout mice, which exhibit a hyperproliferative phenotype in multiple tissues and are more susceptible to tumor development than wild-type animals (Fero et al., 1996; Kiyokawa et al., 1996; Nakayama et al., 1996; Besson et al., 2006; Fero et al., 1998)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to mouse model studies.

claim: p27 is frequently lost in many types of cancers.
source: While the tumor suppressive role of p27 is confirmed by the frequent loss of p27 expression in many types of cancers
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: p27 is mislocalized in a fraction of tumors due to activation of various signaling pathways that cause its nuclear export and/or cytoplasmic retention.
source: p27 is also mislocalized in a fraction of tumors due to activation of various signaling pathways that cause its nuclear export and/or cytoplasmic retention (Chu et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Cytoplasmic p27 has been associated with decreased patient survival in several tumor types including breast carcinomas.
source: Cytoplasmic p27 has been associated with decreased patient survival, high tumor grade and metastasis in several tumor types including breast carcinomas, acute myeloid leukemia, glioblastoma, melanoma and non-small cell lung carcinomas (Lin et al., 2016; Chu et al., 2008; Liang et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2011; Min et al., 2004; Cheng et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: Mice expressing p27CK- mutant are more susceptible than p27-null and wild-type mice to both spontaneous and induced tumor development.
source: These mice are more susceptible than p27-null and wild-type mice to both spontaneous and induced tumor development, thus uncovering an oncogenic role for p27 in vivo (Serres et al., 2011; Besson et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to mouse model studies.

claim: p27 is a multifunctional protein involved in the regulation of multiple cellular processes.
source: It now appears that p27 is a multifunctional protein involved in the regulation of multiple cellular processes, some of which are regulated by p27 in a CDK-independent manner (Besson et al., 2008; Sharma and Pledger, 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles.

claim: p27 has been implicated in the control of cell migration, transcriptional repression, autophagy, stem cell specification and differentiation, cytokinesis, and apoptosis.
source: Indeed, p27 has been implicated in the control of cell migration, transcriptional repression, autophagy, stem cell specification and differentiation, cytokinesis, and apoptosis (Besson et al., 2008; Sharma and Pledger, 2016; Baldassarre et al., 2005; Besson et al., 2004b, 2007; Pippa et al., 2012; Serres et al., 2012; Nickeleit et al., 2008; Liang et al., 2007; Li et al., 2012; Nguyen et al., 2006; Jeannot et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: p27's functional versatility may stem from its intrinsically disordered structure.
source: This functional versatility may stem from the intrinsically disordered structure of p27, which folds upon binding to other proteins, allowing p27 to interact with a wide variety of partners (Lacy et al., 2004; Galea et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Metastasis is the leading cause of cancer related death.
source: Metastasis, the process whereby cells from a primary tumor disseminate throughout the body and form secondary tumors at distant sites, is the leading cause of cancer related death (Sethi and Kang, 2011)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Metastasis requires tumor cells to migrate and invade through neighboring tissues, enter the blood flow and then extravasate to disseminate and form new tumors in host tissues.
source: It requires tumor cells to migrate and invade through neighboring tissues, enter the blood flow and then extravasate to disseminate and form new tumors in host tissues (Sethi and Kang, 2011)
evidence: This is established knowledge about the metastatic process supported by citation.

claim: Regulation of cell motility was the first CDK-independent role ascribed to p27.
source: Regulation of cell motility was the first CDK-independent role ascribed to p27 (Nagahara et al., 1998; Denicourt et al., 2007; Besson et al., 2004b)
evidence: Supported by citations to early studies on p27 and cell motility.

claim: In the cytosol, p27 can interact with RhoA, preventing RhoA activation by guanine-nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs).
source: In the cytosol, p27 can interact with RhoA, preventing RhoA activation by guanine-nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) and thereby modulating actin cytoskeleton dynamics and migration (Besson et al., 2004a, 2004b)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mouse embryo fibroblasts (MEFs) lacking p27 have more RhoA activity, increased numbers of stress fibers and focal adhesions and exhibit a defect in migration.
source: Consequently, mouse embryo fibroblasts (MEFs) lacking p27 have more RhoA activity, increased numbers of stress fibers and focal adhesions and exhibit a defect in migration (Besson et al., 2004b)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The p27-RhoA pathway is important for proper migration of bone marrow macrophages and developing cortical neurons and for cancer cell migration and invasion in vivo.
source: This pathway is important for proper migration of bone marrow macrophages and developing cortical neurons and for cancer cell migration and invasion in vivo (Godin et al., 2012; Nguyen et al., 2006; Papakonstanti et al., 2007; Gui et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2006; See et al., 2010; Larrea et al., 2009; Jin et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to in vivo studies.

claim: p27 can regulate cell migration by controlling microtubule stability through Stathmin or directly by binding to microtubules and promoting microtubule polymerization.
source: p27 can also regulate cell migration by controlling microtubule stability through Stathmin or directly by binding to microtubules and promoting microtubule polymerization (Baldassarre et al., 2005; Godin et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In a 3D environment, cells adopt different strategies to migrate and invade through surrounding matrix.
source: In a 3D environment, cells adopt different strategies to migrate and invade through surrounding matrix (Petrie and Yamada, 2016; Sethi and Kang, 2011)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: RhoA activity favors an amoeboid migration, whereas Rac1 activity promotes mesenchymal migration.
source: The mode of migration is influenced, at least in part, by the activities of Rho GTPases: RhoA activity favors an amoeboid migration, whereas Rac1 activity promotes mesenchymal migration (Sahai and Marshall, 2003; Vial et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cytoplasmic p27 promotes mesenchymal migration via the inhibition of RhoA activity.
source: Accordingly, cytoplasmic p27 promotes mesenchymal migration via the inhibition of RhoA activity, while cells lacking p27 tend to adopt an amoeboid mode of migration (Gui et al., 2014; Belletti et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: p27 was reported to promote epithelial to mesenchymal transition by binding to JAK2, promoting STAT3 activation and the upregulation of Twist1.
source: More recently, p27 was reported to promote epithelial to mesenchymal transition by binding to JAK2, promoting STAT3 activation and the upregulation of Twist1 (Zhao et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Invadosomes are thought to allow cells to coordinate ECM degradation with migration within the tissue microenvironment.
source: Invadosomes (designating both invadopodia and podosomes) are thought to allow cells to coordinate ECM degradation with migration within the tissue microenvironment (Murphy and Courtneidge, 2011; Linder et al., 2011; Di Martino et al., 2016)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cortactin plays a key role in the formation of actin protrusive structures such as lamellipodia and invadosomes.
source: Cortactin plays a key role in the formation of actin protrusive structures such as lamellipodia and invadosomes (Murphy and Courtneidge, 2011; Kirkbride et al., 2011; MacGrath and Koleske, 2012)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cortactin has been involved in all steps of the invadosome lifecycle, from assembly, maturation, proteolytic activity and disassembly.
source: Cortactin has been involved in all steps of the invadosome lifecycle, from assembly, maturation, proteolytic activity and disassembly (MacGrath and Koleske, 2012; Murphy and Courtneidge, 2011; Moshfegh et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: All steps of invadosome lifecycle appear to be regulated by phosphorylation events on Cortactin.
source: All these steps appear to be regulated by phosphorylation events on Cortactin (Oser et al., 2009; Moshfegh et al., 2014; Murphy and Courtneidge, 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cortactin is a scaffold protein composed of an N-terminal acidic domain, followed by several actin-binding repeats, a Pro-rich region and a SH3 domain.
source: Overall, Cortactin is a scaffold protein composed of an N-terminal acidic domain, followed by several actin-binding repeats allowing its interaction with F-actin, a Pro-rich region and a SH3 domain (MacGrath and Koleske, 2012; Kirkbride et al., 2011)
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Phosphorylation of Cortactin by Src and Abl family tyrosine kinases releases the actin severing protein Cofilin from an inhibitory interaction with Cortactin and generates actin barbed ends.
source: Phosphorylation of Cortactin by Src and Abl family tyrosine kinases has two effects: first, this releases the actin severing protein Cofilin from an inhibitory interaction with Cortactin and generates actin barbed ends; second, Arp2/3, N-WASP and Nck1 are recruited onto Cortactin, promoting the polymerization of branched actin (Oser et al., 2009; Weaver et al., 2002; Oser et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Phosphorylation of Cortactin by Src and Abl family tyrosine kinases recruits Arp2/3, N-WASP and Nck1 onto Cortactin, promoting the polymerization of branched actin.
source: Phosphorylation of Cortactin by Src and Abl family tyrosine kinases has two effects: first, this releases the actin severing protein Cofilin from an inhibitory interaction with Cortactin and generates actin barbed ends; second, Arp2/3, N-WASP and Nck1 are recruited onto Cortactin, promoting the polymerization of branched actin (Oser et al., 2009; Weaver et al., 2002; Oser et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Dephosphorylation of Cortactin allows the inhibition of Cofilin activity and stabilizes the invadopodia.
source: Dephosphorylation of Cortactin then allows the inhibition of Cofilin activity and stabilizes the invadopodia (Oser et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Cortactin plays a key role in matrix metalloproteinase secretion in mature invadopodia.
source: Cortactin also plays a key role in matrix metalloproteinase secretion in mature invadopodia (Clark et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Invadopodia disassembly is induced by sequential activation of the Rac-GEF Trio, Rac1 and p21-Activated Kinase-1 (PAK1) pathway.
source: Finally, invadopodia disassembly is induced by sequential activation of the Rac-GEF Trio, Rac1 and p21-Activated Kinase-1 (PAK1) pathway and presumably by PAK1-mediated phosphorylation of Cortactin on Ser113, since a Ser113 to Ala mutant blocked invadopodia disassembly (Moshfegh et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: A Cortactin Ser113 to Ala mutant blocked invadopodia disassembly.
source: Finally, invadopodia disassembly is induced by sequential activation of the Rac-GEF Trio, Rac1 and p21-Activated Kinase-1 (PAK1) pathway and presumably by PAK1-mediated phosphorylation of Cortactin on Ser113, since a Ser113 to Ala mutant blocked invadopodia disassembly (Moshfegh et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: PAK-phosphorylated Cortactin mediates invadopodia disassembly possibly due to decreased affinity of Cortactin phosphorylated within its F-actin binding repeats for F-actin.
source: How PAK-phosphorylated Cortactin mediates invadopodia disassembly is still unclear but could be due, at least in part, to a decreased affinity of Cortactin phosphorylated within its F-actin binding repeats (on S113, S150 and/or S282) for F-actin, potentially destabilizing the structure (Webb et al., 2006, 2005)
evidence: This is speculation based on previous studies cited.

claim: p27 binds to Cortactin in HEK 293 cells overexpressing p27 and Myc-tagged Cortactin.
source: We confirmed the binding of p27 to Cortactin in HEK 293 cells overexpressing p27 and Myc-tagged Cortactin (Figure 1A)
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiment shown in Figure 1A.

claim: p27 binds to Cortactin on endogenous proteins in Hela cells and MEFs immortalized with the human papilloma virus E6 protein.
source: as well as on endogenous proteins in Hela cells and MEFs immortalized with the human papilloma virus E6 protein (Figure 1B) (Serres et al., 2011)
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiment shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Cortactin binds to the p27CK- mutant that cannot interact with cyclins and CDKs.
source: Cortactin bound to the p27CK- mutant, that cannot interact with cyclins and CDKs (Besson et al., 2006, 2007)
evidence: Demonstrated by pull-down assay shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cortactin binds to the C-terminal half (aa 88–198) of p27 but not the N-terminal half (aa 1–87).
source: and to the C-terminal half (aa 88–198) of p27 but not the N-terminal half (aa 1–87) of the protein that contains the cyclin and CDK interaction domains (Figure 1C and D)
evidence: Demonstrated by pull-down assays shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: The Cortactin interaction domain on p27 was narrowed down to the last 8 aa of p27.
source: The Cortactin interaction domain on p27 was narrowed down to the last 8 aa of p27, as a p27CK- 1–190 mutant did not interact with Cortactin any longer (Figure 1E)
evidence: Demonstrated by pull-down assay shown in Figure 1E.

claim: A p27CK- 1–197 mutant, lacking only the C-terminal threonine residue, still bound to Cortactin.
source: A p27CK- 1–197 mutant, lacking only the C-terminal threonine residue, still bound to Cortactin (Figure 1E)
evidence: Demonstrated by pull-down assay shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Phosphorylation on T198 is not needed for p27 binding to Cortactin.
source: suggesting that phosphorylation on T198 is not needed for binding to Cortactin
evidence: Inferred from the observation that p27CK- 1-197 mutant still binds Cortactin.

claim: p27 interacts with the N-terminal half of Cortactin, within the actin binding repeats.
source: These experiments revealed that p27 interacts with the N-terminal half of Cortactin, within the actin binding repeats, as a mutant Cortactin lacking the actin binding repeats 3 to 6 (ΔABR3-6) did not bind p27 (Figure 1F)
evidence: Demonstrated by pull-down assays with Cortactin deletion mutants shown in Figure 1F.

claim: p27 colocalizes with Tks5 in invadopodia in p27+/+E6 MEFs.
source: In these conditions, p27 could be readily observed in invadopodia where it colocalized with Tks5, a commonly used invadopodia marker (Seals et al., 2005), or Cortactin (Figure 2A and B, respectively)
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 2A.

claim: p27 colocalizes with Cortactin in invadopodia in p27+/+E6 MEFs.
source: In these conditions, p27 could be readily observed in invadopodia where it colocalized with Tks5, a commonly used invadopodia marker (Seals et al., 2005), or Cortactin (Figure 2A and B, respectively)
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 2B.

claim: p27 localizes to invadopodia in human A549 lung adenocarcinoma and A375 melanoma cell lines.
source: The same approach was used to confirm p27 localization to invadopodia in human A549 lung adenocarcinoma and A375 melanoma cell lines (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Invadopodium and podosome formation is stimulated by growth factors.
source: Invadopodium and podosome formation is stimulated by growth factors (Murphy and Courtneidge, 2011)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Growth factor stimulation causes the degradation of p27 as cells enter the cell cycle.
source: Growth factor stimulation causes the degradation of p27 as cells enter the cell cycle but also the relocalization of a fraction of p27 in the cytoplasm between 1 hr and 6 hr post-stimulation, dependent on the phoshorylation of p27 on Ser10 (Besson et al., 2006, 2004b; Boehm et al., 2002; Ishida et al., 2002; Rodier et al., 2001; Connor et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Growth factor stimulation causes the relocalization of a fraction of p27 in the cytoplasm between 1 hr and 6 hr post-stimulation, dependent on the phosphorylation of p27 on Ser10.
source: Growth factor stimulation causes the degradation of p27 as cells enter the cell cycle but also the relocalization of a fraction of p27 in the cytoplasm between 1 hr and 6 hr post-stimulation, dependent on the phoshorylation of p27 on Ser10 (Besson et al., 2006, 2004b; Boehm et al., 2002; Ishida et al., 2002; Rodier et al., 2001; Connor et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: E6 immortalized MEF lines form functional, matrix degrading invadopodia.
source: We first verified that the E6 immortalized MEF lines used in our study were forming functional, matrix degrading invadopodia. For this, p27+/+, p27−/− and p27CK-/CK- E6 MEFs were seeded on fluorescent gelatin and Tks5 immunostaining indicated that these cells could all form Tks5-containing structures that efficiently degraded gelatin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Demonstrated by gelatin degradation assay shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: p27 colocalizes with Tks5 at sites of gelatin degradation in MEFs and A549 cells.
source: p27 colocalized with Tks5 at sites of gelatin degradation in MEFs and A549 cells, suggesting that p27 can be present at functional invadopodia (Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cells expressing p27 or p27CK- rarely form invadopodia (5.83% and 8.68%, respectively).
source: Counting of the number of cells forming invadopodia using Tks5 immunostaining (Figure 3A) revealed that while cells expressing p27 or p27CK- rarely formed invadopodia (5.83% and 8.68%, respectively)
evidence: Quantified from Tks5 immunostaining shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Nearly half of MEFs lacking p27 have invadopodia (44.66%).
source: nearly half of MEFs lacking p27 had invadopodia (44.66%) (Figure 3B)
evidence: Quantified from Tks5 immunostaining shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: p27−/− cells have a dramatically increased capacity to degrade ECM compared to p27+/+ and p27CK-/CK- MEFs.
source: In keeping with the number of invadopodia forming cells, measurement of the area of fluorescent gelatin degraded per cell showed that p27−/− cells had a dramatically increased capacity to degrade ECM compared to p27+/+ and p27CK-/CK- MEFs (Figure 3C and D)
evidence: Quantified from gelatin degradation assay shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Expression of WT p27 and p27CK- significantly decreased both the number of p27−/− cells forming invadopodia and their capacity to degrade gelatin.
source: Quantification of the number of cells forming invadopodia and of the area of gelatin degraded per cell indicated that expression of WT p27 and p27CK- significantly decreased both the number of p27−/− cells forming invadopodia and their capacity to degrade gelatin, while the p27CK- 1–190 mutant had no effect (Figure 3F and G)
evidence: Demonstrated by rescue experiments shown in Figure 3F-G.

claim: The p27CK- 1–190 mutant had no effect on invadopodia formation or gelatin degradation in p27−/− cells.
source: Quantification of the number of cells forming invadopodia and of the area of gelatin degraded per cell indicated that expression of WT p27 and p27CK- significantly decreased both the number of p27−/− cells forming invadopodia and their capacity to degrade gelatin, while the p27CK- 1–190 mutant had no effect (Figure 3F and G)
evidence: Demonstrated by rescue experiments shown in Figure 3F-G.

claim: The domain mediating p27's interaction with Cortactin is required for p27's function in limiting invadopodia formation.
source: Thus, our data suggests that p27 limits invadopodia formation and that the domain mediating its interaction with Cortactin is required for this function.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that p27CK- 1-190 mutant, which cannot bind Cortactin, has no effect on invadopodia.

claim: p27−/− cells have a migration defect in 2D scratch wound assays.
source: We compared the motility of p27+/+, p27−/− and p27CK-/CK- E6 MEFs in 2D scratch wound assays and p27−/− cells had a migration defect (Figure 4A and B), in agreement with our previous findings (Besson et al., 2004b)
evidence: Demonstrated by scratch wound assay shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: 3D invasion is reduced in p27−/− MEFs compared to either WT p27 or p27CK- expressing cells.
source: We next measured the capacity of these MEFs to invade through a layer of Collagen I in transwell inserts. Similar to 2D migration, 3D invasion was reduced in p27−/− MEFs compared to either WT p27 or p27CK- expressing cells (Figure 4C and D)
evidence: Demonstrated by transwell invasion assay shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: p27CK- restored invasion of p27−/− cells while the p27CK- 1–190 mutant had no effect.
source: To confirm the involvement of p27 in regulating invasion, p27−/− E6 MEFs retrovirally infected with either empty vector, p27CK- or p27CK- 1–190 (Figure 4E, left panel) were subjected to transwell invasion assays. While p27CK- restored invasion of p27−/− cells, the p27CK- 1–190 mutant had no effect (Figure 4E, right panel)
evidence: Demonstrated by rescue experiments shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Although p27 limits the number of invadopodia in MEFs, it also promotes cellular invasion through ECM.
source: Taken together our results indicate that although p27 limits the number of invadopodia in MEFs, it also promotes cellular invasion through ECM.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: While p27-null cells more frequently form invadopodia and exhibit an increased capacity to degrade ECM, their ability to invade through matrix is significantly impaired.
source: On the other hand, while p27-null cells more frequently form invadopodia and exhibit an increased capacity to degrade ECM, their ability to invade through matrix was significantly impaired.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Inhibition of Rac1, Trio or PAK1 with siRNAs causes a dramatic increase in invadopodia lifetime and in their capacity to degrade matrix, but this is accompanied by a sharp decrease in cell invasion.
source: Interestingly, a similar, seemingly paradoxical finding was recently reported, in which inhibition of Rac1, Trio or PAK1 with siRNAs caused a dramatic increase in invadopodia lifetime and in their capacity to degrade matrix, but this was accompanied by a sharp decrease in cell invasion (Moshfegh et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Activation of the Trio/Rac1/PAK1 pathway induced a putative PAK1-mediated phosphorylation of Cortactin and invadopodia disassembly.
source: In this study, activation of the Trio/Rac1/PAK1 pathway induced a putative PAK1-mediated phosphorylation of Cortactin and invadopodia disassembly, as expression of a S113A Cortactin mutant blocked this pathway (Moshfegh et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Altering the dynamics of invadopodia turnover inhibits invasion.
source: In this study, altering the dynamics of invadopodia turnover inhibited invasion (Moshfegh et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Invadopodia lifetime is on average 16.7 min in p27+/+ cells.
source: Videomicroscopy analyses revealed that while invadopodia lifetime was on average 16.7 min in p27+/+ cells
evidence: Measured by live cell imaging shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Invadopodia mean duration is 65.9 min in p27−/− cells.
source: their mean duration was 65.9 min in p27−/− cells (Figure 5A)
evidence: Measured by live cell imaging shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Invadopodia appear more stable in cells lacking p27.
source: Thus, invadopodia appear more stable in cells lacking p27.
evidence: Inferred from the increased invadopodia lifetime in p27-null cells.

claim: The presence of p27 increases the amount of Cortactin co-immunoprecipitated with PAK1 in Hela cells.
source: In contrast, the presence of p27 increased the amount of Cortactin co-immunoprecipitated with PAK1 in Hela cells (Figure 5B)
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In MEFs lacking p27, the amount of Cortactin co-precipitated with PAK1 is sharply decreased compared to p27+/+ cells.
source: Conversely, in MEFs lacking p27, the amount of Cortactin co-precipitated with PAK1 was sharply decreased compared to p27+/+ cells, despite the fact that PAK1 levels were elevated in p27−/− cells (Figure 5C)
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation shown in Figure 5C.

claim: PAK1 levels are elevated in p27−/− cells.
source: Conversely, in MEFs lacking p27, the amount of Cortactin co-precipitated with PAK1 was sharply decreased compared to p27+/+ cells, despite the fact that PAK1 levels were elevated in p27−/− cells (Figure 5C)
evidence: Observed in immunoblots shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Some PAK1 is already associated with Cortactin in serum starved cells.
source: Monitoring the kinetics of association of PAK1 with Cortactin in MEFs revealed that some PAK1 is already associated with Cortactin in serum starved cells, consistent with a previous report (Vidal et al., 2002)
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation time course shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: PAK1 association with Cortactin progressively increases after serum stimulation, reaching a maximal level after 3 hr.
source: and progressively increase after serum stimulation, reaching a maximal level after 3 hr (Figure 5D and E)
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation time course shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: p27 binding to Cortactin promotes the association of PAK1 with Cortactin.
source: These results suggest that p27 binding to Cortactin promotes the association of PAK1 with Cortactin.
evidence: Inferred from the co-IP experiments showing increased PAK1-Cortactin interaction in presence of p27.

claim: PAK1 and p27 colocalize at structures resembling invadopodia.
source: Immunostaining of p27+/+ MEFs showed a colocalization of PAK1 and p27 at structures resembling invadopodia (Figure 5F)
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 5F.

claim: p27 overexpression in Hela cells has no effect on the interaction of Cortactin with c-Src, ERK1 or Arp2.
source: p27 overexpression in Hela cells had no effect on the interaction of Cortactin with c-Src, ERK1 or Arp2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) (Kirkbride et al., 2011)
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cortactin acetylation levels do not change when p27 is overexpressed.
source: Also, Cortactin acetylation levels did not change when p27 was overexpressed (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblot shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: PAK1 silencing dramatically increases both the number of cells forming invadopodia and the area of matrix degraded per cell in p27+/+ MEFs.
source: While PAK1 silencing or the PAK1-3 inhibitors dramatically increased both the number of cells forming invadopodia and the area of matrix degraded per cell in p27+/+ MEFs, as reported previously (Moshfegh et al., 2014), it had no effect in p27−/− cells (Figure 6A–B,D–F, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B)
evidence: Demonstrated by siRNA experiments shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: PAK1 silencing has no effect on invadopodia formation or matrix degradation in p27−/− cells.
source: While PAK1 silencing or the PAK1-3 inhibitors dramatically increased both the number of cells forming invadopodia and the area of matrix degraded per cell in p27+/+ MEFs, as reported previously (Moshfegh et al., 2014), it had no effect in p27−/− cells (Figure 6A–B,D–F, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B)
evidence: Demonstrated by siRNA experiments shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: PAK1-3 inhibitors dramatically increase both the number of cells forming invadopodia and the area of matrix degraded per cell in p27+/+ MEFs.
source: While PAK1 silencing or the PAK1-3 inhibitors dramatically increased both the number of cells forming invadopodia and the area of matrix degraded per cell in p27+/+ MEFs, as reported previously (Moshfegh et al., 2014), it had no effect in p27−/− cells (Figure 6A–B,D–F, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B)
evidence: Demonstrated by inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 6D-F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: PAK1-3 inhibitors have no effect on invadopodia formation or matrix degradation in p27−/− cells.
source: While PAK1 silencing or the PAK1-3 inhibitors dramatically increased both the number of cells forming invadopodia and the area of matrix degraded per cell in p27+/+ MEFs, as reported previously (Moshfegh et al., 2014), it had no effect in p27−/− cells (Figure 6A–B,D–F, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B)
evidence: Demonstrated by inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 6D-F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: p27 acts downstream of PAK1 in the regulation of invadopodia formation and activity.
source: These results suggest that p27 acts downstream of PAK1 in the regulation of invadopodia formation and activity, and that this pathway is impaired in p27−/− cells, possibly due to decreased PAK1/Cortactin interaction.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that PAK1 inhibition has no effect in p27-null cells.

claim: There is no difference in Rac1 activation levels in p27+/+ and p27−/− cells.
source: If p27 acts on the invadopodia disassembly pathway at the level of PAK1/Cortactin, one would not expect to see any difference in Rac1 activation levels in p27+/+ and p27−/− cells. This is what was observed by GTP-Rac1 pull-down assays (Figure 7A), in agreement with our previous observations (Besson et al., 2004b)
evidence: Demonstrated by Rac1-GTP pull-down assay shown in Figure 7A.

claim: When Rac1 is silenced or inhibited, more p27+/+ cells form invadopodia and there is a dramatic increase in the area of matrix degraded.
source: When Rac1 was silenced or inhibited, more p27+/+ cells formed invadopodia and there was a dramatic increase in the area of matrix degraded (Figure 7B,E and C,F, respectively), as reported previously (Moshfegh et al., 2014)
evidence: Demonstrated by Rac1 siRNA and inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 7B-C, E-F.

claim: In p27−/− cells, Rac1 silencing or inhibition has no effect on invadopodia formation or gelatin degradation.
source: On the other hand, in p27−/− cells, Rac1 silencing or inhibition had no effect on invadopodia formation or gelatin degradation (Figure 7B,E and C,F, respectively)
evidence: Demonstrated by Rac1 siRNA and inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 7B-C, E-F.

claim: p27 regulates invadopodia disassembly downstream of Rac1 and PAK1.
source: supporting the idea that p27 regulates invadopodia disassembly downstream of Rac1 and PAK1
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Rac1 inhibition has no effect in p27-null cells.

claim: Transfection of RhoA siRNAs in p27+/+ and p27−/− MEFs does not alter the proportion of cells forming invadopodia.
source: Transfection of RhoA siRNAs in p27+/+ and p27−/− MEFs did not alter the proportion of cells forming invadopodia (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Demonstrated by RhoA siRNA experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RhoA siRNAs only mildly increase the ability of both p27+/+ and p27−/− cells to degrade ECM, although this is not statistically significant.
source: and only mildly increased the ability of both p27+/+ and p27−/− cells to degrade ECM, although this was not statistically significant (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Demonstrated by RhoA siRNA experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Inhibition of ROCK1/2 does not affect the ability of p27+/+ and p27−/− cells to invade through Collagen I in transwell invasion assays.
source: Furthermore, inhibition of the Rho effectors ROCK1/2 with a pharmacological inhibitor (Y27632) did not affect the ability of p27+/+ and p27−/− cells to invade through Collagen I in transwell invasion assays (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: Demonstrated by ROCK inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: In MEFs, depletion of RhoA does not affect the ability of cells to form invadopodia.
source: Thus, in MEFs, depletion of RhoA did not affect the ability of cells to form invadopodia and slightly increased invadopodia proteolytic activity independently of p27 status.
evidence: Concluded from RhoA siRNA experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Depletion of RhoA slightly increases invadopodia proteolytic activity independently of p27 status.
source: Thus, in MEFs, depletion of RhoA did not affect the ability of cells to form invadopodia and slightly increased invadopodia proteolytic activity independently of p27 status.
evidence: Concluded from RhoA siRNA experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Invadopodia disassembly by the Trio/Rac1/PAK1 signaling pathway is mediated by phosphorylation of Cortactin on Ser113.
source: Evidence suggests that invadopodia disassembly by the Trio/Rac1/PAK1 signaling pathway is mediated by phosphorylation of Cortactin on Ser113 (Webb et al., 2005; Moshfegh et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Expression of Cortactin S113A increases both invadopodia lifetime and matrix degradation.
source: In the latter study, expression of an unphosphorylatable mutant of Cortactin (Cortactin S113A) increased both invadopodia lifetime and matrix degradation, as observed upon Rac1 or PAK1 silencing (Moshfegh et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: In p27+/+ cells, Cortactin S113A increases the number of cells forming invadopodia.
source: In p27+/+ cells, Cortactin S113A increased the number of cells forming invadopodia, as observed previously (Moshfegh et al., 2014), while Cortactin S113D had no effect (Figure 8B and D)
evidence: Demonstrated by Cortactin mutant experiments shown in Figure 8B.

claim: In p27+/+ cells, Cortactin S113D has no effect on invadopodia formation.
source: In p27+/+ cells, Cortactin S113A increased the number of cells forming invadopodia, as observed previously (Moshfegh et al., 2014), while Cortactin S113D had no effect (Figure 8B and D)
evidence: Demonstrated by Cortactin mutant experiments shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Cortactin S113A has no effect in p27−/− cells.
source: In contrast, Cortactin S113A had no effect in p27−/− cells, confirming that the Rac1/PAK1/Cortactin pathway is defective in absence of p27 and that p27 acts upstream of Cortactin.
evidence: Demonstrated by Cortactin mutant experiments shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The Rac1/PAK1/Cortactin pathway is defective in absence of p27.
source: In contrast, Cortactin S113A had no effect in p27−/− cells, confirming that the Rac1/PAK1/Cortactin pathway is defective in absence of p27 and that p27 acts upstream of Cortactin.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Cortactin S113A has no effect in p27-null cells.

claim: p27 acts upstream of Cortactin in the invadopodia disassembly pathway.
source: In contrast, Cortactin S113A had no effect in p27−/− cells, confirming that the Rac1/PAK1/Cortactin pathway is defective in absence of p27 and that p27 acts upstream of Cortactin.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Cortactin S113A has no effect in p27-null cells.

claim: Expression of Cortactin S113D in p27−/− cells decreases the number of invadopodia forming cells and the area of degraded gelatin.
source: On the other hand, expression of Cortactin S113D in p27−/− cells decreased the number of invadopodia forming cells and the area of degraded gelatin (Figure 8C and E)
evidence: Demonstrated by Cortactin mutant experiments shown in Figure 8C and E.

claim: Mimicking Cortactin phosphorylation rescues the phenotype caused by the absence of p27.
source: indicating that mimicking Cortactin phosphorylation rescues the phenotype caused by the absence of p27
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Cortactin S113D rescues the p27-null phenotype.

claim: PAK3 phosphorylates Cortactin on several serine residues (S113, S150 and S282) within the actin binding repeats.
source: Importantly, PAK3 was reported to phosphorylate Cortactin on several serine residues (S113, S150 and S282) within the actin binding repeats (Webb et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Multiple phosphorylation events on Cortactin may synergize to regulate Cortactin function.
source: suggesting that multiple phosphorylation events may synergize to regulate Cortactin function
evidence: This is speculation based on the previous finding that PAK3 phosphorylates multiple sites.

claim: Cortactin TA and TD mutants give essentially similar results as the Cortactin S113A and S113D mutants, respectively.
source: Cortactin TA and TD mutants gave essentially similar results as the Cortactin S113A and S113D mutants, respectively (Figure 8G–J)
evidence: Demonstrated by Cortactin triple mutant experiments shown in Figure 8G-J.

claim: In p27+/+ MEFs, the Cortactin TA mutant is more potent than Cortactin S113A to promote invadopodia formation.
source: Nevertheless, in p27+/+ MEFs, the Cortactin TA mutant was more potent than Cortactin S113A to promote invadopodia formation (13.5% p27+/+ cells forming invadopodia with Cortactin S113A versus 23.3% with Cortactin TA) and activity (6.17 fold increase in area of degraded gelatin with Cortactin S113A versus 10.02 fold with Cortactin TA) (Figure 8B versus Figure 8G and Figure 8D versus Figure 8I, respectively)
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing Cortactin S113A and TA mutant effects shown in Figure 8.

claim: Cortactin phosphorylation on S150 and/or S282 also contribute with S113 to control invadopodia disassembly.
source: This data suggests that Cortactin phosphorylation on S150 and/or S282 also contribute with S113 to control invadopodia disassembly.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that the triple mutant is more potent than the S113A mutant alone.

claim: In presence of FRAX597, there is a 36% decrease in P-Ser Cortactin level.
source: In presence of FRAX597, there was a 36% decrease in P-Ser Cortactin level (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B)
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblot shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Cortactin is a substrate for other Ser/Thr kinases such as ERK, Akt and PKC.
source: This mild reduction in P-Ser levels is consistent with Cortactin also being a substrate for other Ser/Thr kinases such as ERK, Akt and PKC.
evidence: This is established knowledge used to interpret the data.

claim: P-Ser levels are reduced in Cortactin S113A immunoprecipitations compared to WT Cortactin.
source: P-Ser levels were reduced in Cortactin S113A immunoprecipitations compared to WT Cortactin and further decreased in Cortactin TA immunoprecipitates, confirming that phosphorylation of these sites contribute to the Cortactin P-Ser signal in vivo (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblot shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: P-Ser levels are further decreased in Cortactin TA immunoprecipitates compared to Cortactin S113A.
source: P-Ser levels were reduced in Cortactin S113A immunoprecipitations compared to WT Cortactin and further decreased in Cortactin TA immunoprecipitates, confirming that phosphorylation of these sites contribute to the Cortactin P-Ser signal in vivo (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblot shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Phosphorylation of S113, S150 and S282 contribute to the Cortactin P-Ser signal in vivo.
source: P-Ser levels were reduced in Cortactin S113A immunoprecipitations compared to WT Cortactin and further decreased in Cortactin TA immunoprecipitates, confirming that phosphorylation of these sites contribute to the Cortactin P-Ser signal in vivo (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblot shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Cortactin is phosphorylated on S150 in vivo.
source: MS/MS analyses from Cortactin immunoprecipitates indicated that Cortactin was phosphorylated on S150 (Figure 8—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Demonstrated by mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cortactin S150 phosphorylation is detected only in samples from cells co-expressing Cortactin and Myr-SH3-2.
source: This phosphorylation was detected only in samples from cells co-expressing Cortactin and Myr-SH3-2 suggesting that PAK1 activation is required for this event.
evidence: Observed in mass spectrometry experiments.

claim: PAK1 activation is required for Cortactin S150 phosphorylation.
source: This phosphorylation was detected only in samples from cells co-expressing Cortactin and Myr-SH3-2 suggesting that PAK1 activation is required for this event.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that S150 phosphorylation is only detected when PAK1 is activated.

claim: Cortactin is phosphorylated in vivo on S113 in prostate cancer cells, mouse brain and breast cancers.
source: Although no phosphorylation was detected on S113 or S282 in these experiments, phosphoproteome analyses from other studies have previously shown that Cortactin is phosphorylated in vivo on S113, S150 and/or S282: S113 phosphorylation was detected in prostate cancer cells (Chen et al., 2010), mouse brain (Wiśniewski et al., 2010) and breast cancers (Mertins et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to phosphoproteome studies.

claim: Cortactin S150 phosphorylation was identified in mouse renal cells and human liver.
source: Phosphorylation on S150 was identified in mouse renal cells and human liver (Bian et al., 2014; Rinschen et al., 2010) and in the present study.
evidence: Supported by citations to phosphoproteome studies and the current study.

claim: Cortactin S282 phosphorylation was detected in mitotic cells and breast cancers.
source: S282 phosphorylation was detected in mitotic cells and breast cancers (Mertins et al., 2016; Olsen et al., 2010; Klammer et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to phosphoproteome studies.

claim: Phosphorylation on all three sites (S113, S150, S282) have been detected in ovarian and breast cancer xenografts.
source: Phosphorylation on all three sites have been detected in ovarian and breast cancer xenogratfs (Mertins et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to phosphoproteome study.

claim: p27 regulates invadopodia formation and activity by binding to Cortactin, probably via the regulation of invadopodia turnover mediated by the Trio/Rac1/PAK1/Cortactin pathway.
source: Our results indicate that p27 regulates invadopodia formation and activity by binding to Cortactin, probably via the regulation of invadopodia turnover mediated by a signaling pathway recently characterized whereby signaling through Trio/Rac1/PAK1/Cortactin induces the disassembly of invadopodia (Moshfegh et al., 2014)
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study supported by the experimental data.

claim: p27 directly controls cellular invasion by impinging on the Trio/Rac1/PAK1/Cortactin pathway through the promotion of the Cortactin/PAK1 interaction and the phosphorylation of Cortactin on Ser113, S150 and/or S282 by PAK.
source: The main finding presented here is that p27 directly controls cellular invasion by impinging on this pathway through the promotion of the Cortactin/PAK1 interaction and the phosphorylation of Cortactin on Ser113, S150 and/or S282 by PAK.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study supported by the experimental data.

claim: Inhibiting the Rac1/PAK1/Cortactin pathway upstream of Cortactin converts the phenotype of p27+/+ cells to that of p27−/− cells.
source: Indeed, inhibiting the pathway upstream of Cortactin, either with Rac1 and PAK1 inhibitors or siRNAs converted the phenotype of p27+/+ cells to that of p27−/− cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Artificially activating the Rac1/PAK1/Cortactin pathway at the level of Cortactin using phosphomimetic mutants efficiently rescues the phenotype of p27-null cells.
source: Conversely, artificially activating this pathway at the level of Cortactin using phosphomimetic mutants for the PAK-targeted sites efficiently rescued the phenotype of p27-null cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments in Figure 8.

claim: All three phosphorylation sites on Cortactin (S113, S150, S282) act synergistically.
source: All three phosphorylation sites on Cortactin appear to act synergistically as the phenotype caused by the triple mutants (Cortactin TA and TD) was more profound than that of mutating S113 alone.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing single and triple mutants in Figure 8.

claim: Mimicking the phosphorylation of Cortactin on PAK1-targeted sites causes the disassembly of invadopodia.
source: While mimicking the phosphorylation of Cortactin on PAK1-targeted sites clearly causes the disassembly of invadopodia (Moshfegh et al., 2014; Webb et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The mechanism by which phosphorylated Cortactin causes invadopodia disassembly may be due to decreased affinity of Cortactin phosphorylated within its Actin-binding repeats for F-Actin.
source: the mechanism involved is still unclear but may be due to decreased affinity of Cortactin phosphorylated within its Actin-binding repeats for F-Actin, which may destabilize invadopodia (Webb et al., 2006)
evidence: This is speculation based on previous studies.

claim: Inhibition of the Trio/Rac1/PAK1/Phospho-Cortactin pathway stabilizes invadopodia and is associated with a dramatic increase in proteolytic degradation of ECM.
source: Results from Moshfegh et al. (2014) and the present study show that inhibition of the Trio/Rac1/PAK1/Phospho-Cortactin pathway stabilizes invadopodia and is associated with a dramatic increase in proteolytic degradation of ECM.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study and previous work.

claim: Stabilization of invadopodia is accompanied by a sharp decrease in the ability of cells to invade through matrix in 3D invasion assays.
source: Surprisingly, this phenotype is accompanied by a sharp decrease in the ability of cells to invade through matrix in 3D invasion assays.
evidence: Demonstrated by invasion assays in Figure 4.

claim: The turnover of invadopodia rather than elevated ECM degradation is required for efficient invasion.
source: Thus, it appears that the turnover of invadopodia rather than elevated ECM degradation is required for efficient invasion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that increased invadopodia stability correlates with decreased invasion.

claim: Affecting the dynamics of invadopodia formation, maturation and disassembly is detrimental to invasion.
source: Affecting the dynamics of invadopodia formation, maturation and disassembly is therefore detrimental to invasion, as observed here when this last step is inhibited by interfering with Rac1/PAK1 signaling or when p27 is absent.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: p27 regulates cell migration by interfering with RhoA activation by its GEFs.
source: Interestingly, p27 also regulates cell migration in a similar manner by interfering with RhoA activation by its GEFs (Besson et al., 2004a, 2004b)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In absence of p27, cells accumulate actin stress fibers and focal adhesions and exhibit a migration defect due to an imbalance in the dynamic cycles of RhoA activation and inactivation.
source: In absence of p27, cells accumulate actins stress fibers and focal adhesions and exhibit a migration defect due to an imbalance in the dynamic cycles of RhoA activation and inactivation (and concomitant Rac1 inactivation and activation) required for F-actin turnover, focal adhesion disassembly and efficient migration (Besson et al., 2004a, 2004b; Ren et al., 2000; Arthur and Burridge, 2001; Cox et al., 2001; Sahai et al., 2001; Vial et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Migration and invasion are two intimately linked processes.
source: Migration and invasion are two intimately linked processes (Friedl and Wolf, 2003; Petrie and Yamada, 2016)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: p27 regulates both migration and invasion by distinct mechanisms.
source: It is quite remarkable that p27 appears to regulate both of these processes, although by distinct mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study and previous work.

claim: p27 binds to RhoA and Cortactin via the same domain located within the last 8 aa of the protein.
source: Indeed, p27 binds to RhoA and Cortactin via the same domain located within the last 8 aa of the protein (Figure 1E) (Larrea et al., 2009; Godin et al., 2012)
evidence: Demonstrated by mapping experiments in Figure 1E and supported by citations.

claim: RhoA preferentially binds p27 phosphorylated on T198.
source: but while RhoA preferentially binds p27 phosphorylated on T198 (Larrea et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The interaction of p27 with Cortactin does not require the presence of T198.
source: the interaction of p27 with Cortactin did not require the presence of T198 (Figure 1E)
evidence: Demonstrated by pull-down assay in Figure 1E.

claim: Different pools of p27 are involved in the regulation of RhoA and Cortactin.
source: suggesting that different pools of the protein are involved in their regulation
evidence: Inferred from the differential requirement for T198 in binding to RhoA versus Cortactin.

claim: The regulation of invadopodia by p27 does not appear to involve RhoA.
source: In addition, the regulation of invadopodia by p27 did not appear to involve RhoA, as RhoA silencing affected both p27−/− and p27+/+ cells in a similar manner (Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Demonstrated by RhoA siRNA experiments in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: p27 regulates invasion by promoting EMT, notably through JAK2/STAT3 signaling and induction of the transcription factor Twist.
source: p27 also regulates invasion by promoting EMT, notably through JAK2/STAT3 signaling and induction of the transcription factor Twist (Zhao et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Cortactin is an intrinsically disordered protein (IDP), especially its actin-binding repeats.
source: Evidence suggest that Cortactin is an intrinsically disordered protein (IDP), especially its actin-binding repeats (Shvetsov et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: p27 is a well-known intrinsically disordered protein (IDP).
source: and p27 is a well-known IDP (Galea et al., 2008; Lacy et al., 2004; Ou et al., 2012)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Intrinsically disordered proteins typically fold upon binding to their partners.
source: Since these proteins typically fold upon binding to their partners
evidence: This is established knowledge about IDPs.

claim: p27 binding may cause a conformation change in Cortactin that would favor its interaction with PAK1.
source: an attractive possibility is that p27 binding causes a conformation change in Cortactin that would favor its interaction with PAK1
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism by which p27 promotes PAK1-Cortactin interaction.

claim: p27 regulates migration and invasion in a CDK-independent manner.
source: p27 is a cyclin-CDK inhibitor and although p27 regulates migration and invasion in a CDK-independent manner (Besson et al., 2004b; Larrea et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2015; Gui et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Some cell cycle independent roles of CDKs and cyclins may be mediated via CDK inhibitors such as p27.
source: there is evidence to suggest that some cell cycle independent roles of CDKs and cyclins may be mediated via CDK inhibitors such as p27 (Hydbring et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to review article.

claim: The regulation of cell migration by Cyclin D1 requires p27.
source: For instance, the regulation of cell migration by Cyclin D1 requires p27 (Li et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The role of CDK5 in promoting neuronal progenitor migration in vivo is mediated via the phosphorylation of p27 on Ser10.
source: and the role of CDK5 in promoting neuronal progenitor migration in vivo is mediated via the phosphorylation of p27 on Ser10 which regulates the RhoA/ROCK/LIMK/Cofilin pathway (Nguyen et al., 2006; Kawauchi et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CDK5 plays an important role in invadopodia formation and cancer cell invasion.
source: Interestingly, CDK5 was recently found to play an important role in invadopodia formation and cancer cell invasion, and CDK5 inhibition blocked both these processes (Quintavalle et al., 2011; Bisht et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CDK5 phosphorylates Caldesmon, causing its degradation by the proteasome and promoting invadopodia formation and invasion.
source: CDK5 phosphorylated Caldesmon, causing its degradation by the proteasome and promoting invadopodia formation and invasion (Quintavalle et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: p27 is a poor inhibitor of CDK5 complexes.
source: Since p27 is a poor inhibitor of CDK5 complexes (Lacy et al., 2005; Lee et al., 1996)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: p27 could simultaneously interact with CDK5 complexes via its N-terminal cyclin-CDK binding domain and with Cortactin via its C-terminus, thereby recruiting CDK5 in proximity to Caldesmon bound to Cortactin.
source: Indeed, an attractive hypothesis is that p27 could simultaneously interact with CDK5 complexes, via its N-terminal cyclin-CDK binding domain, and with Cortactin via its C-terminus, thereby recruiting CDK5 in proximity to Caldesmon bound to Cortactin and allowing Caldesmon phosphorylation.
evidence: This is speculation about a potential mechanism involving p27, CDK5, and Cortactin.

claim: The Cdkn1b gene is rarely mutated in cancer.
source: Our study further defines the complex role played by p27 in the regulation of cytoskeletal dynamics, migration, EMT and invasion and provides another element to explain why the Cdkn1b gene is rarely mutated in cancer (Chu et al., 2008; Besson et al., 2008; Kandoth et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: p27 is either downregulated, mostly via increased proteasomal degradation, or excluded from the nuclei of cancer cells.
source: Indeed, p27 is either downregulated, mostly via increased proteasomal degradation, or excluded from the nuclei of cancer cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about p27 in cancer.

claim: Upon cytoplasmic relocalization, p27 promotes both migration and invasion and may serve to coordinately regulate these processes.
source: Given that upon cytoplasmic relocalization, p27 promotes both migration and invasion and may serve to coordinately regulate these processes
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study and previous work.

claim: Cytoplasmic p27 may be selected for during tumor progression and could participate in the acquisition of a metastatic behavior by cancer cells.
source: it appears likely that this feature may be selected for during tumor progression and could participate in the acquisition of a metastatic behavior by cancer cells
evidence: This is speculation about the clinical implications of the findings.
